one_liner: Pure-Rust big integers that beat GMP (via rug) only on one-word (<=64-bit) values and on string parsing.
what_it_does: ibig provides UBig (unsigned) and IBig (signed) arbitrary-precision integers with Rust operator overloading, ubig!/ibig! literal macros, radix parsing and formatting (bases 2-36), pow, gcd/extended gcd, and a ModuloRing/Modulo type for modular arithmetic. It is a Rust crate with no C ABI, so it is not a replacement for GMP's mpz_t in C or C++ code; from Rust it replaces rug or num-bigint at the type level, with a different API.
how_it_is_fast: UBig is an enum: Small(Word) holds a value that fits in one machine word inline, and only longer values allocate a Buffer, so one-word arithmetic avoids the heap allocation that rug/mpz pays per result. Multiplication switches from schoolbook (<=24 words) to Karatsuba (<=192 words) to Toom-3; division is schoolbook below 32 words and recursive divide-and-conquer above; non-power-of-two parsing works in 256-word chunks combined with precomputed radix powers. On x86-64 limb add/sub use the _addcarry_u64/_subborrow_u64 intrinsics; there is no hand-written assembly.
when_to_use: Rust code where most values fit in 64 bits but must not overflow (counters, exact rationals with small parts, property-test shrinkers): one-word add/sub/mul/div measured 1.5-2.1 ns vs 17.7-28.3 ns for rug
Parsing many decimal or hex strings into big integers: ubig_from_hex and ubig_from_dec beat rug at every size up to 10^4 bits
Targets where linking GMP is impractical or LGPL is unacceptable: pure Rust, no_std, MIT OR Apache-2.0
Embedded or wasm builds that need big integers without a C toolchain
when_not_to_use: Operands of two words or more: rug/GMP is already ahead at 100 bits on add, sub and div, and about 2.8x faster on 10^4-bit multiplication (4.52 us vs 12.69 us)
gcd-heavy or modular-inverse-heavy code: gcd is a binary (quadratic) algorithm, 16x slower than rug at 10^4 bits (850.52 us vs 53.05 us) and 111x slower on extended gcd (7.82 ms vs 70.31 us)
Large computations (millions of digits): multiplication stops at Toom-3 with no FFT/NTT path in the released code; ibig's own suite has 10M digits of e at 20.673 s vs rug 2.788 s
Converting big values to strings: ubig_to_hex at 10^4 bits is 7.34 us vs rug 2.47 us
C or C++ projects: there is no C API; use dashu or malachite only if you are in Rust anyway, otherwise GMP itself

integration.dependencies: ibig 0.3.6: cfg-if, static_assertions, num-traits (no_std); optional rand 0.8, serde 1.0
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.49 for the crates.io 0.3.6 release (crates.io rust_version); the repo's ibig-old copy now declares 1.93 and the unreleased 0.4.0 rewrite needs 1.95 (edition 2024)
integration.platforms: any Rust target; x86 and x86-64 get carry intrinsics, other targets use generic 16/32/64-bit word code
integration.thread_safety: not documented; UBig/IBig are plain owned values and no global mutable state was seen in the source read

gotchas: The repository's main code (ibig 0.4.0 on ibig-core) is a from-scratch rewrite its README calls 'in early development'; the benchmarked and published code is 0.3.6 (2022-09-17), kept in ibig-old/, so the GitHub HEAD and the crate differ
Only one word is stored inline: 65-128-bit values (u128, i128) already allocate, e.g. ubig_from_u128 21.4 ns vs dashu 1.8 ns
UBig is capped at UBig::MAX_BIT_LEN (close to usize::MAX bits) and panics if exceeded; gcd(0, 0) panics
Issue #18 ('0 shouldn't have a modular inverse') was closed in November 2022, after the last release; whether 0.3.6 is affected is not documented
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Prefer dashu (a hard fork of ibig) in almost every case: it also inlines two-word values, has a subquadratic gcd (13x faster than ibig at 10^4 bits) and is within a few percent of ibig on add, mul and parsing at 1,000-10^4 bits in the same report. Pick ibig only for its smaller, frozen, permissively licensed 0.3.6 codebase; pick malachite or rug when operands exceed about 1,000 bits, and Boost.Multiprecision fixed cpp_int or ctbignum from C++.
verified_claims_summary: In DRMacIver's third-party Criterion suite (rustc 1.92.0, default bench profile, Apple M2 Max), ibig 0.3.6 beat rug 1.30.0/GMP on 10-bit add/sub/mul/div (1.5-2.1 ns vs 17.7-28.3 ns) and on hex/decimal parsing at all sizes, but lost to rug from 100 bits up on add/sub/div and at 10^4 bits on mul, gcd, pow, modular ops and formatting. The small-value win comes from avoiding a per-result heap allocation, not from faster limb kernels.
status_note: The repo is active (commits in July 2026) but on an unreleased rewrite; the crate has had no release since 0.3.6 in September 2022, still draws about 118k recent downloads, and is MIT OR Apache-2.0, small and pure Rust, so the old version is easy to vendor.
